metadata.title: Evaluating scientific thinking among Shanghai’s students of high and low-performing schools

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study collected primary data from two purposively selected schools in the greater Shanghai region (one high-performing school and one low-performing school) and administered specially designed, previously validated science-thinking assessments to 15-year-old 9th-grade students. The manuscript does not report the use of any complex survey design weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures, and the analysis is based on small, school-based samples rather than an international probability sample. Because the outcomes are scored from custom tasks (CoV, multivariable causal reasoning, and multivariable analysis/prediction) and the paper does not describe any weighting variables, the results should be interpreted as descriptive comparisons between two schools rather than population-representative estimates. No PV scaling or ILSA score scaling is involved; the weighting guidance here is therefore limited to noting that no survey-weight variable was applied in the reported analyses.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variables are performance scores derived from specially designed assessments (e.g., correct/consistent CoV comparisons, coded causal-reasoning categories, and prediction correctness) rather than ILSA cognitive achievement scales that use PVs. The paper also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., exclusion rules or imputation), which is a reporting gap for transparency, especially given the small sample size.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample comprised 55 fifteen-year-old 9th-grade students: 26 from one high-performing school in downtown Shanghai and 29 from one low-performing school in the outskirts of Jinshan district. Inclusion was based on school identity (HPS vs LPS) and age/grade (15-year-olds, 9th grade). The study does not report additional item-level exclusions, missing-response rules, or any imputation; tasks were administered as graded activities on different days, with teacher facilitation and pilot testing after translation into Mandarin.

main_findings.dataset_used: Custom CoV scientific thinking assessment (Shanghai; 15-year-olds, Grade 9; science reasoning)
main_findings.target_variable: Control of Variables (CoV) skills (consistent controlled comparison + justification)
main_findings.performance_metrics: HPS: 24/26 (92%) consistently constructed a controlled comparison across three cases (X2(1)=0.525, p=0.469). HPS: 22/26 (84%) also provided appropriate justifications (X2(1)=0.035, p=0.853). LPS: 26/29 (90%) and 25/29 (86%) respectively; no significant differences between schools.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the Custom CoV scientific thinking assessment data from Shanghai 15-year-olds (Grade 9), the study compared performance between students from a high-performing school and a low-performing school on CoV skills, finding that both schools performed exceptionally well with no significant between-school differences in controlled comparisons or justifications. This indicates that Shanghai’s science curriculum and instruction may effectively develop CoV-based scientific reasoning across both high- and low-performing schools, though the evidence is limited to two schools and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: Custom multivariable causal reasoning assessment (Shanghai; 15-year-olds, Grade 9; science reasoning)
main_findings.target_variable: Multivariable causal reasoning (coded causal-variable identification and context comparison)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multivariable category (any multivariable causal reasoning): 7/26 (27%) HPS vs 5/29 (17%) LPS (p=0.517, Fisher’s exact test). Context comparison (inner city vs outlying neighborhoods): 10/26 (38%) HPS vs 7/29 (24%) LPS (p=0.381, Fisher’s exact test). Table 1 shows most responses were no-variable or single-variable categories in both schools.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the Custom multivariable causal reasoning assessment data from Shanghai 15-year-olds (Grade 9), the study compared high- vs low-performing school students on multivariable causal reasoning, finding that most students relied on single-variable or no-variable explanations and that only a minority demonstrated multivariable reasoning or context comparison. This indicates that Shanghai’s instruction may strengthen univariable/CoV causal thinking more than multivariable causal reasoning, suggesting a need for curriculum and teaching that explicitly trains students to coordinate multiple causes and compare contexts, while noting the small two-school sample limits generalizability.

main_findings.dataset_used: Custom multivariable analysis and prediction assessment (Shanghai; 15-year-olds, Grade 9; science reasoning/prediction)
main_findings.target_variable: Multivariable analysis and prediction skills (correct predictions + correct contributing/noncontributing factor attributions across nine countries)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Correct prediction score (0–9 model): HPS mean=7.8 (SD=1.51) vs LPS mean=7.2 (SD=1.78), t=0.322, p=0.714. Correctly predicted all nine countries: 6/26 (23%) HPS vs 5/29 (17%) LPS (p=0.739, Fisher’s exact test). Contributing-factor totals: HPS mean=21.7 (SD=5.46) vs LPS mean=22.5 (SD=5.78), t=-0.539, p=-0.592 (as reported). Noncontributing factor (Country Size) attribution: HPS mean=2.7 (SD=0.80) vs LPS mean=3.0 (SD=1.30), t=-0.958, p=0.354. Consistency choosing all four contributing factors across nine predictions: 7/26 (27%) HPS vs 5/29 (17%) LPS (p=0.517, Fisher’s exact test).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the Custom multivariable analysis and prediction assessment data from Shanghai 15-year-olds (Grade 9), the study compared high- vs low-performing school students on multivariable prediction performance and factor attribution, finding no significant between-school differences but overall comparatively weak multivariable reasoning (limited consistent selection of all contributing factors and nontrivial selection of the noncontributing factor). This indicates that strengthening multivariable causal modeling and prediction training—beyond CoV-style single-cause reasoning—may be important for improving students’ readiness for authentic scientific practice, though causality cannot be inferred from this small, non-random two-school design.

data.outcome_summary: This study used specially designed, previously validated science-thinking assessments administered to 55 Shanghai 15-year-old Grade 9 students from two schools (one high-performing and one low-performing). The outcomes were not ILSA PV-based achievement scores; instead, they were scored from (1) a Control of Variables (CoV) task requiring consistent controlled comparisons and justifications, (2) a multivariable causal reasoning task coded into causal-variable categories and context-comparison behavior, and (3) a multivariable analysis/prediction task requiring correct predictions across nine countries and correct attribution of contributing vs noncontributing factors. Across all three tasks, there were no statistically significant between-school differences (e.g., CoV controlled comparisons: X2(1)=0.525, p=0.469; prediction score: t=0.322, p=0.714). However, multivariable causal reasoning and prediction performance were comparatively weak, with most students favoring single-variable explanations and showing limited consistency in selecting all contributing factors. The paper does not report any missing-data handling strategy and does not use survey weights, so results should be interpreted cautiously and cannot be generalized to all Shanghai students.
